newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Penang plans new infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Penang plans new infrastructure.

text.p: Penang plans a slew of infrastructure projects to retain its attraction for multinational electronics firms and foreign tourists, the northern island state's Chief Minister Koh Tsu Koon says.
He told Reuters late on Wednesday that growing labour costs and crowding on the island known as "Malaysia's Silicon Valley" were a concern, but the problems were under control.

The 40-year-old leader, the only ethnic Chinese chief minister among Malaysia's 13 states, said infrastructure plans included a $1.0 billion bridge across the strait to the mainland, highways and tourist attractions.

The mostly Japanese and American electronics firms that have given Penang its nickname are not being driven out by higher costs but were instead planning less labour-intensive and higher-technology projects.

"It is true we are no longer a cheap labour centre, but the nature of the industry has also changed because, in the meantime, they have moved to greater automation. And the skill content of our workforce has also changed," Koh said.
He did not say how high wages have risen, but sources in Penang's electronics industry said labour costs were growing at 10 to 15 percent annually.
"It is true some of the more labour intensive operations are moving out. We encourage them to move out," Koh said.
"We are undergoing a transition that Singapore and Hong Kong underwent a few years ago successfully. If we do our job well we will also under go a successful transformation."

But unless the state kept wage increases under check, maintained political stability and kept infrastructure upgraded, it could lose out to countries with a more plentiful labour pool such as the Philippines and Indonesia, he said.
Penang-based companies have expressed confidence in the state by making new investments, Koh said.
"This is reflected by the fact that last year a survey of 353 major factories in Penang showed a reinvestment of three billion ringgit ($1.2 billion) in 1996," he said.
The Malaysian Industrial Development Authority last year approved 97 new investment projects for Penang with a total investment of 3.1 billion ringgit, against 1.6 billion in 1995.

Koh said Packard Bell-NEC has located its manufacturing and customer sales service centre for Asia-Pacific in Penang. Last year Dell Computer Corp opened a $20 million plant to service its Asia-Pacific customers.
In addition, recent investments have also come from Acer Inc, Intel Corp and Motorola Inc
After nearly a year in the doldrums, Malaysia's electronic exports have staged a strong recovery so far in 1997, Koh said.
"We are seeing a pick-up (in electronic exports) in the last two quarters, starting at the end of 1996," he added.
He did not give any figures, saying the government did not collect such data from manufacturers.

A sharp drop last year in the growth of the electronics industry, Malaysia's biggest exporter, slowed the fast-growing economy. Gross domestic product growth dipped to 8.2 percent in 1996 against 9.5 percent in 1995.
Electronics account for around 40 percent of the country's exports. They include semi-conductors, computers, peripherals, disc drives as well as consumer products such as audio and video equipment.
($1=2.5 ringgit)
